nameStory: The Chestnut Longhorn Beetle gets its name from its rich, chestnut-brown coloring that resembles the warm hues of chestnuts fresh from the shell. Like all longhorn beetles, it sports impressively long antennae that can stretch as long as or longer than its entire body, giving it that distinctive 'longhorn' appearance that makes this beetle family so recognizable.
description: The Chestnut Longhorn Beetle is a medium-sized beetle with a sleek, elongated body dressed in warm chestnut-brown tones. These beetles typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with their most striking feature being their exceptionally long, thread-like antennae. Their bodies have a somewhat flattened appearance and a smooth, polished look that catches the light beautifully. You'll most often spot them on flowers during summer months, where they feed on pollen and nectar.

idTips.label: Long Antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are extremely long and thread-like, often as long as the entire body or longer, with a smooth texture when gently touched

idTips.label: Chestnut Coloring
idTips.description: Body displays rich chestnut-brown to reddish-brown coloration with a glossy, polished appearance that reflects light

idTips.label: Elongated Body
idTips.description: Body is narrow and elongated rather than round, with a slightly flattened profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Flower Feeding
idTips.description: Often found with their head buried deep in flowers, particularly white or yellow blooms, feeding on pollen and nectar

idTips.label: Smooth Texture
idTips.description: Body surface feels smooth and hard to the touch, lacking the fuzzy hairs or rough bumps found on many other beetles

habitat: Look for Chestnut Longhorn Beetles in sunny forest edges, meadows, and gardens where wildflowers bloom abundantly. They're particularly drawn to areas with a mix of deciduous trees and open flowering spaces, from sea level up into the mountains. You'll often find them in the same spots where elderflowers, wild roses, and other native blooms attract pollinators.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but are not yet commonly seen. Look for early individuals on the first warm days when flowers start blooming.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time! Adults are most active and visible on flowers during warm, sunny days. This is the best season for identification and observation.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down significantly. Most individuals have completed their life cycle, though a few stragglers may still appear on late-blooming flowers.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not present. Larvae are developing inside dead wood, completely hidden from view until the following year.

funFact: Despite being called longhorn beetles, these insects are actually important pollinators that rival bees in their effectiveness at transferring pollen between flowers - their long antennae and fuzzy bodies pick up pollen as they crawl deep into blooms searching for nectar!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other brown longhorn beetles, but the Chestnut Longhorn's rich, uniform chestnut-brown color sets it apart from species with black markings or lighter colors. Remember: 'Chestnut smooth and brown, other longhorns wear a frown' - meaning other species often have more complex color patterns or markings.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'cordifera' means 'heart-bearing,' likely referring to some heart-shaped marking or structure, though this may not be easily visible to casual observers. This species was first scientifically described way back in 1795, making it one of the earlier beetles to be formally recognized by science.
compareHints: Since this is the only Judolia species in our New England dataset, compare it to other brown longhorn beetles in the region. The Chestnut Longhorn's uniform chestnut-brown color and medium size distinguish it from the larger, more variable brown longhorns, and its smooth body texture separates it from the more heavily marked or bumpy species. Its flower-feeding behavior is also more pronounced than many of its wood-boring relatives.
